did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with the heading “A psalm of Asaph” and presents a direct appeal to God in response to the defilement of the temple and the destruction of Jerusalem.
Did you know? Jerusalem is described with the words “They have reduced Jerusalem to ruins”—that is, the city was destroyed and left in ruins.

Did you know? The psalmist portrays the desecration of the dead with a vivid and disturbing image: the bodies of God’s servants and faithful people were given as food to the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth.
Did you know? This verse emphasizes the depth of the catastrophe: blood was poured out around Jerusalem “like water,” and there was no one to bury the dead.

Did you know? In the middle of the description of destruction comes a question expressing expectation: “How long?” It conveys the feeling of ongoing suffering and the psalmist’s plea for God’s anger to end.
Did you know? The people do not claim to be innocent; instead, they ask, “Do not hold against us the sins of past generations”—a plea for mercy despite the sins of the past.
Did you know? The request for deliverance is twice justified by concern for God’s honor: “for the glory of your name” and “for the sake of your name,” not merely by the people’s needs.

Did you know? The psalmist asks God to act in the sight of the nations, so that the vengeance for the blood of his servants will be known and an answer will be given to the question, “Where is their God?”
Did you know? The expression “sevenfold” expresses the psalmist’s request that God repay the neighboring nations many times over for the disgrace with which they taunted him.

Did you know? The conclusion moves from destruction to hope and faithfulness: Israel is called “your people, the sheep of your pasture,” and commits to proclaiming God’s praise from generation to generation.
